groups.title: Password security and cryptographic hashing
groups.question: Your MERN app stores user passwords and gives logged-in users a JWT. Explain how passwords should be stored so a stolen database doesn't reveal them, and what a JWT contains and protects.

followUps.Why bcrypt uses work factor and salting: Why does bcrypt use a salt and a cost factor, and why not just hash the password with SHA-256?
followUps.JWT structure: header, payload, and sign: Anyone can decode a JWT's payload. So what does the signature protect, and how does the server check it?

evidence.text: bcrypt adds a random salt per password, so identical passwords get different hashes and precomputed tables don't work.
Its cost factor makes each hash deliberately slow, so guessing passwords at scale is very expensive, and it can be raised as hardware gets faster.
At login the entered password is hashed and compared; the original password is never stored or decrypted.

notEnough: Only saying hash passwords with bcrypt without explaining the salt or the slowness.

misconceptions.text: Says passwords should be encrypted so they can be decrypted later.

evidence.text: A JWT has a header, a payload of claims and a signature, each Base64URL-encoded and joined by dots.
The payload is only encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can read it; passwords and secrets never go there.
The server recomputes the signature from the header and payload with its secret; if it doesn't match, the token was changed and is rejected.

notEnough: Only saying a JWT has three parts without saying what the signature does.

misconceptions.text: Says the JWT payload is encrypted and safe for sensitive data.

groups.title: HTTP-only cookies versus localStorage for token storage
groups.question: You need to decide where your React app keeps the auth token, knowing that a comment field might let an attacker inject a script, and that other sites might try to make requests to your API. Explain your choice and the attacks it defends against.

followUps.Why XSS can steal localStorage tokens bu: Why can an injected script steal a token from localStorage but not from an HTTP-only cookie?
followUps.CSRF attacks and SameSite cookie attribu: Cookies are sent automatically, so what is CSRF, and how does SameSite help?

evidence.text: Any script running on the page, including an injected one, can read localStorage and send the token away.
JavaScript can't read an HTTP-only cookie, so the token is sent with requests but can't be stolen by the script.

notEnough: Only saying cookies are safer than localStorage without explaining why.

misconceptions.text: Says HTTP-only cookies stop XSS attacks from happening at all.

evidence.text: CSRF makes a logged-in user's browser send a request to your API from another site, and the browser attaches the cookie automatically.
The SameSite attribute stops the cookie from being sent on cross-site requests (Strict) or most of them (Lax), which blocks that attack.

notEnough: Only saying use SameSite without explaining what CSRF is.

groups.title: Implementing JWT auth in Express
groups.question: Users log in to your Express API and then call protected endpoints like creating a post. Explain how the server issues tokens at login, how long they last, and how each protected request is checked.

followUps.Signing and verifying JWTs with jsonwebt: Why always set expiresIn, and how does a refresh token keep the user logged in?
followUps.Auth middleware: extracting and verifyin: Walk through what the auth middleware does with the Authorization header, and what happens if the token has expired.

evidence.text: At login the server signs a token with a secret, containing claims like the user id, plus an expiry.
A short expiry limits how long a stolen token can be used.
A longer-lived refresh token, kept in an HTTP-only cookie, is used to get new access tokens without logging in again.

notEnough: Only saying sign a token with jsonwebtoken without explaining expiry or refresh.

evidence.text: The middleware reads the Bearer token from the Authorization header.
It verifies the signature and the expiry with the secret, and rejects the request with 401 if that fails.
On success it attaches the decoded user to req and calls next(), and it's applied only to the routes that need auth.

notEnough: Only saying check the token in a middleware without the steps.

misconceptions.text: Says decoding the token is enough without verifying its signature.

groups.title: CORS and input sanitization
groups.question: Your React app on one domain calls your API on another, and a security review found that users can open other users' orders by changing the id in the URL. Explain how you'd configure cross-origin access and fix the most common security holes.

followUps.Configuring cors middleware with an orig: Why restrict the cors origin to your frontend's URL, and why can't you use '*' with cookies?
followUps.OWASP Top 10 essentials: injection, brok: What is IDOR, and how would you fix the orders endpoint? Name another OWASP risk relevant to MongoDB.

evidence.text: Browsers block a page from reading responses from another origin unless the API allows that origin in its CORS headers.
The API should allow only its own frontend's origins, not every site.
When requests carry cookies, the allowed origin must be named exactly; a wildcard isn't allowed with credentials.

notEnough: Only saying enable cors without explaining what it controls.

misconceptions.text: Says CORS protects the API from requests made by scripts or tools like curl.

evidence.text: IDOR means the API returns or changes an object just because its id was given, without checking that it belongs to the user.
The fix is to check on the server that the logged-in user owns or may access that object.
Injection also applies to MongoDB: passing raw request objects into queries lets attackers add operators like $ne, so input must be validated.

notEnough: Only naming OWASP Top 10 items without explaining any of them.
